title: Cloze test: the village library
text:
Read the passage and choose the most appropriate word for each numbered blank.

Reading is a habit that grows with practice. A small library that opened in our village last year has (1) ........ the lives of many children. Earlier, they had (2) ........ to read except their school textbooks. Now they borrow a new book every week and (3) ........ the stories with their friends. The librarian, a retired teacher, (4) ........ them to write short reviews of what they read. Many parents say their children have become more (5) ........ and now ask questions about everything they see.

title: Reading comprehension: the dabbawalas of Mumbai
text:
Every working day, thousands of dabbawalas in Mumbai collect home-cooked lunches from kitchens across the city and deliver them to offices before the lunch hour. Most of them have little formal schooling, and for more than a century they have worked without computers. Instead, the lid of each tiffin box carries a short code of letters, numbers and colours. The code tells a dabbawala where the box was picked up, which railway station it must reach and which building it must be delivered to.

A single box may pass through the hands of three or four dabbawalas in one journey, yet mistakes are said to be extremely rare. Visitors from business schools have studied the system to learn how simple rules, teamwork and punctuality can work better than costly technology. After lunch, the empty boxes travel back along the same route and reach home by evening.

title: Cloze test: the post office
text:
Read the passage and choose the most appropriate word for each numbered blank.

The postman was once the most awaited visitor in every Indian home. Letters (1) ........ news of births, weddings and examination results. Today most messages travel (2) ........ mobile phones within seconds. Yet the post office has not lost its (3) ......... It now delivers parcels from online shops and (4) ........ savings accounts for people in remote villages. In many hill and forest areas it remains the only bank within (5) ........ distance.

title: Reading comprehension: the return of millets
text:
Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the everyday grains of rural India. They grow well on poor soil, need far less water than rice, and can survive long dry spells. Over the decades, however, many farmers switched to wheat and rice, which were supported by irrigation and assured government buying. As a result, millets slowly disappeared from city kitchens.

In recent years, doctors and nutrition experts have pointed out that millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and release their energy slowly. Some state governments now add them to school meals and ration supplies. Farmers in dry districts, who struggle when the rains fail, may gain the most if the demand for these hardy grains keeps rising.
